278.t: Replacing Huey Smith with Shirley and Lee
278.s: He took Huey Smith's place on the road with Shirley and Lee; he praises Huey's authentic influence.
278.q: Not alternating with it. I took Huey's place. Huey's records had begun to do very well. So it was time for him to go on his own. I went to take his place, whether it would be temporarily or permanent, and it ended up in being permanent, the first trip. So we weren't alternating, actually.

278.t: Formal piano training and early influences
278.s: Toussaint had only a couple of months of formal lessons; he lists Fats Waller, Professor Longhair, Ray Charles and others as favorite pianists.
278.q: I liked all records, all the records that are out here. And I liked Ranky Tank type pianos. I liked Fats Waller. I liked Professor Longhair, of course. Ray Charles. Lloyd Glenn. Albert Hammond. By Albert Hammond. Fuck like that.

618.t: Early piano influences: Shearing, Tatum, Billy Taylor, Peterson
618.s: He names the pianists who shaped him, from Shearing and Tatum to Billy Taylor at the Streamliner and Oscar Peterson with Ray Brown.
618.q: Oh yeah. I mean I think most musicians start off being mostly affected by people on their instrument and then they expand their auditory interests. For me the very first jazz piano album I can recall hearing was an album my piano teacher brought me, it was a ten inch MGM LP called “You’re Hearing…

618.t: Encouragement from Billy Taylor, George Russell and Bill Evans
618.s: He recounts three pivotal meetings: Billy Taylor at his home, studying the Lydian concept with Russell, and Bill Evans critiquing his first trio album.
618.q: on the near west side. And again, because I was tall I could get in there, and I remember just spending nights listening to the Billy Taylor Trio and it just was wonderful music. Then I got a chance to hear Oscar Peterson at the London House in Chicago, which used to be a wonderful supper club. And…

104.t: Milt Buckner and Nat Cole as origins of block chords
104.s: Williams credits Milt Buckner and Nat Cole with the block style; she heard Cole records in USO day rooms in Germany along with Stan Kenton and Loumell Morgan.
104.q: Had a very good trio, sort of like the poor man’s Nat Cole.

104.t: Younger pianists: Herbie Hancock, Chick Corea and Roy Haynes
104.s: She names Herbie Hancock's tunes and Chick Corea's 'Now He Sings, Now He Sobs' among favourites and praises Roy Haynes for keeping up with the times.
104.q: All those people. All those people. I’ve got probably an LP upstairs of Herbie playing “Watermelon Man.” That’s what I remember about him. And certain points . . . certain records of his that I liked a lot. Tunes like “Maiden Voyage” and “Tell Me a Bedtime Story.” There’s a bunch of things.

662.t: Other pianists and lack of influences
662.s: She admires pianist Ruby May Townsend, a schoolteacher. No records or players influenced her; she wanted her own style.
662.q: One of my friends, whom I've mentioned, the pianist, the pianist whom I've mentioned, a farmer. I especially liked Ruby Mae Townsend, she was very good.

196.t: Early influences, the vaudeville trio and Roy Barton
196.s: Leclerc learned from no particular player, liked Joe Burgess, and recalls the vaudeville trio Leclerc, Fitzgerald and McCormick. Allen asks about Roy Barton.
196.ch: Pianists, radio and cafes of old New Orleans
196.q: man no only ones I knew was the ones that I liked were like a little bars off on the Joe Burgess and two or three other things I don't quite remember their names no do you remember Dewey

194.t: Late 1930s: Father Toots and learning from many pianists
194.s: He recalls a floor show around 1938-40, the helper Father Toots and a piano player in Stormy Weather, and says he built his piano style by combining many players.
194.ch: Piano influences and the New Orleans scene
194.q: 19th. What time was that, uh, uh, uh, we were working at the New York Antis. You know, when we had that little flow show.

155.t: Classical pianists he admired and meeting Gene Schroeder and Yank Lawson at Condon's
155.s: Rachmaninoff, de Pachmann, Cortot, then friends such as Dick Hyman, Dick Wellstood, and first meeting Schroeder and Lawson.
155.q: It is, yes. People that I admire that I used to listen to, my mother would have me listen to, was Rachmaninoff, hear him play his own things, and hear, a very interesting guy was DePackman, Vladimir DePackman. And he was a great — he loved to play Chopin music. And in those days records were made…

316.t: Piano influences: Waller, Teddy Wilson and Bud Powell
316.s: Fats Waller and Teddy Wilson first, later bebop and Bud Powell; he later traveled with Wilson.
316.q: Well at the beginning you know since it happened when I was eleven, twelve years old taking those piano lessons, the music that appealed to me most then was the pianists Fats Waller and Teddy Wilson. Really different kinds of pianists but I loved them both. They were both great. Particularly Teddy.…

746.t: How she wants her playing heard; imitating Cecil Taylor and McCoy Tyner
746.s: Crispell wants her playing to be true and organic; she describes imitating Tyner and Cecil Taylor as influences while finding her own voice.
746.q: Gosh. Well I try to play what is true for me, what comes from my heart, and that could be something that is very abstract with a lot of energy, it could be something very romantic, it could be lots of different things. And my hope is that I can travel seamlessly between them and that my voice still…

559.t: Influences of Johnny Smith and Wes Montgomery
559.s: He admired Smith's sound and voicings but was more influenced by Wes Montgomery, heard in Harlem.
559.q: Yeah it was. I loved the sound that he got, I loved the voicings that he got, and I wanted to try to figure out how to do both. The technique I could do, the voicings, my fingers were not as long as his were and not — yeah. I worked — I got one part of it but not both parts. And so I used to listen…

747.t: George Shearing and the first piano influences
747.s: Shearing was his first influence, followed by Billy Taylor, Peterson, Silver and Fats Waller; Jimmy Yancey discovered while copying.
747.q: George Shearing was my very first influence. I used to play “I’ll Remember April,” which his arrangement came out in sheet music. And when I was 13 — I started crossing over into jazz when I was around that age — and I was a professional at 14. But prior to that I was playing that piece. That was…

502.t: Why bebop took singers out of the music; discovering Milestones and McCoy Tyner
502.s: He argues bebop heads gave singers little to sing, preferring the swing era, and was floored by Milestones, Tyner and Corea, which drove him to piano.
502.q: Yeah. Well that’s a big thing to me. Because I think the bebop era took the singers out of the music. All the great singers — Ella and Sarah and Billy Eckstine, all those great singers were in the swing era. And then when bebop came in it got very analytical, very — it’s a brilliant music, and…

748.t: Favorite organists: Jimmy Smith and the turnaround of hearing Larry Young
748.s: Levin names Larry Young and Jimmy Smith, and describes seeing Tony Williams' Lifetime with McLaughlin and Young, which changed how he thought about organ.
748.q: Larry Young. Sometimes I get a lot of coffee and I’m racing and racing, and then my thoughts get left — Larry Young is just amazing. There was a big turnaround for me, I think somewhere in the 70s, because I’d been listening to Jimmy Smith, like everybody, and trying to emulate him, which of course…

749.t: Learning harmony from Walter Bishop Jr. and Don Pullen
749.s: Bishop's harmonic influence and book, Pullen's melodic and avant-garde inside-the-blues approach; she absorbed from the masters.
749.q: This is, you know jazz is such a wonderful experiment where we’re exploring possibilities all the time. It’s the nature of the music you know. And I’m young and I’m anxious and I’m learning and I want to be liked, I want to be known and recognized for being a musician not just a singer myself you…

733.s: Person recalls buying 78s in the South and lists tenor influences led by Illinois Jacquet, plus Archia, Griffin, Mobley, Ammons, Getz, Marsh, Holiday and Percy France; he likes organ and piano groups alike.
733.q: Oh yeah, yeah. Dinah Washington, Buddy Johnson, Stan Kenton. I was in the south. Yeah, Stan Kenton, Dizzy Gillespie. Just about everybody — Lester Young — they were all on 78’s. And then the LP came.

443.t: Tastes: Condon-style swing and favourite players
443.s: College jazz kept him paid and in the Condon-style swing world; he later worked with Wilson, Hackett, Venuti and Goodman, and admired Ruby Braff.
443.q: Well it paid my way through school so I knew it had an economic thing. And Dixieland or New York Swing, Eddie Condon stuff had a resurgence in the ‘50s, and so I stayed with that because it was very popular at all the colleges. And since it was still popular for me, as soon as I graduated college I…

750.t: Piano influences: Mary Lou Williams, boogie woogie, Jimmy Yancey, Leroy Carr
750.s: Her father's boogie-woogie albums and a high-school friend's Jimmy Yancey records shaped her piano style.
750.q: How many hours do we have here? My first well of course Mary Lou Williams and all those boogie woogie guys that — my dad got me these albums — Pinetop Smith and Albert Ammons, and Meade Lux Lewis and on and on. So that really influenced me. But this guy, this guy who I met when I was a junior in…

751.t: Piano influences: Mehegan, Bill Evans and the Detroit players
751.s: Rowe describes studying with John Mehegan, discovering Bud Powell, Monk and Evans, her white upbringing, and revering Barry Harris, Tommy Flanagan and Hank Jones.
751.q: Marian was just, as she was for so many people, especially women players I think, you know a mentor, she always looked out after me and gave me opportunities. I heard her playing a little bit. My parents had some LPs with her on it when I was growing up. But

600.t: Pianist influences: McCoy Tyner, Herbie Hancock, Chick Corea, Keith Jarrett
600.s: Rowe offers names; Rydin says Hancock, Tyner, Corea and Jarrett, plus Bill Evans, shaped his playing.
600.q: Definitely. Definitely. Again, when I was at the age where you think about how you want to play, I had four musicians at the generation of McCoy. It was Herbie Hancock, it was McCoy Tyner, it was Chick Corea and it was Keith Jarrett. And then of course there was always Bill Evans. But I wanted to…

358.t: Favorite pianists: Oscar Peterson's advice at the Blue Note
358.s: Asked for three favorites, Simmons names Ahmad Jamal and Oscar Peterson, who gave him technique advice in 1953 while he was with Flip Phillips and Bill Harris.
358.q: I have to go, I have to go like influence. And I’d have to say that was Ahmad Jamal, and I’d have to say Oscar Peterson, because Oscar actually took the time, Oscar turned the corner for me. In other words prior to Oscar, I was out of that Duke Ellington mode and I was like a background player. I…

219.t: Earl Hines, Teddy Wilson, Pee Wee Russell and the Savoy in Boston
219.s: Wein discusses his piano influences, studying with Teddy Wilson, a long engagement with Pee Wee Russell, Edmond Hall at the Savoy, and the idea of his own club.
219.q: Sam Sax, my teacher, was a disciple of Earl Hines. And in those days of course you didn’t have Bud Powell stamps. Earl Hines was the piano player for the big bands. I loved Teddy Wilson and Earl Hines. Teddy Wilson was a refined version of Earl Hines. Earl Hines played with octaves and tremolos.…

494.t: Piano influences Tommy Flanagan and Hank Jones, and Horace Silver's writing
494.s: Falling for Flanagan's touch on a Miles record, meeting him much later, and admiring Horace Silver's memorable tunes.
494.ch: Philadelphia roots and arrival in New York
494.q: On record, yeah. A friend of mine had a recording. It was a Miles [Davis] record. It was either – I think – I don’t know whether it was Collector’s Items, maybe? But it wasn’t Tommy’s. I think it was Miles’s record. Anyway, they did In Your Own Sweet Way. I remember, boy, I really – Tommy, the…

515.t: Playing along with Bud Powell records
515.s: He describes playing along with Bud Powell recordings and why he did the Remembering Bud Powell project.
515.q: Bud was one of my first... Well, first of all, he was the first pianist I heard on that 78­ vinyl when I was a kid that got me real sparkled about the piano. I wanted to be able to play with that kind of fluidity. So during the ‘60s, one of the things I did with Bud’s music and his

460.t: Models on flute: pianists as inspiration
460.s: Laws says no flute players inspired his improvising; instead pianists such as Chick Corea, Herbie Hancock and McCoy Tyner did, along with Freddie Hubbard.
460.ch: Modern Jazz Sextet, the flute and Los Angeles
460.q: Piano players. Those guys who really impressed me, these guys who have command of all three of the elements of music: rhythm, harmony, and melody. Percussion. Then they have the harmony there. They can sound more than one note at the same time. And the melody too. That was my inspiration. I’ll tell…

589.t: Influences: MJQ, Oscar Peterson, Shearing and other pianists
589.s: Lewis names the Modern Jazz Quartet, Oscar Peterson at London House, George Shearing, Nat Cole, Teddy Wilson and others who shaped him.
589.q: No doubt, the Modern Jazz Quartet. I think the reason was because of John Lewis and the classical thing, and Milt Jackson and the blues. So, there it is, classical and gospel. Milt Jackson, gospel, right? So that was just a natural. But then, Oscar Peterson. Oscar Peterson beat me up. Whoa. It’s…

505.t: Richie Beirach: same neighborhood, quick wit, escaping influences
505.s: Liebman describes his lifelong partnership with Beirach, their shared Brooklyn roots and their search to escape the influence of the great pianists.
505.ch: Beirach, harmony and the dotted feel
505.q: Amazingly, we’re from the same neighborhood, which we did not know. He moved, I think, when he was 9 or 10 years old from 3 blocks away from me in Brooklyn. You know Brooklyn’s alphabet soup, the area. We were in – he’s on P. I’m on M. There you go. He was on 2nd or 3rd Street, and I was on 5th…

565.t: Cachao's mambo, Arsenio Rodriguez and Lili Martinez
565.s: He credits Orestes Lopez's mambo and Arsenio's conjunto, and explains how Lili Martinez and El Viejo Socarron became his mentors.
565.ch: Latin music history and the Palladium
565.q: He wrote a number called “Mambo.” It’s beautiful. [SINGS IT...] Beautiful. And a piano solo by Jesus Lopez that’s frightening. They had already brought in the conga. But the mambo that gets accelerated later is different. But the name “mambo” stays. And Mambo, in the religion, is like a…

117.t: Earl Hines and the influences that make a style
117.s: Freeman credits Earl Hines with introducing the Harlem pianists, and describes his own style as a ball of many influences.
117.ch: Chicago friends: Tesch, Stacy and Wettling
117.q: I wanted to add and I think it is only fair to add, if I did not say this, that Jess was not only influenced by Louis and Bix, but certainly by Earl Hines, as I think we all were. Earl Hines had a style of playing -- now, here, it was Earl Hines who told me about the James P. Johnsons, the Fats…

125.t: Boogie-woogie from Pete Johnson and Albert Ammons; his love for Lester Young
125.s: In New York Johnson and Ammons taught him boogie-woogie; he loved Lester Young, wanted to play tenor, and modelled his piano style on Lester.
125.ch: New York with Lester Young and Coleman Hawkins
125.q: Johnson and Albert Ammons became very influential in my life, and they taught me the boogie-woogie style. And Pete Johnson was a very warm human being. And he and Albert Ammons both. And the fact of the matter is the way I went to New York was I was sent to play with Lester Young, who was my real…
